name: Cyproheptadine appetite protocol

lead: Cyproheptadine is a first-generation antihistamine and serotonin antagonist that increases appetite and weight as a known effect. People in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles discuss it as a way to eat more when they struggle to reach calorie targets, hoping for a fuller, more muscular physique.

A 2019 systematic review of 46 articles found that most studies reported weight gain with cyproheptadine, though in varied populations such as children, people with cystic fibrosis or cancer, and anorexia nervosa patients.

paras: Forum discussions treat it as an appetite aid alongside high-calorie eating and training. It is taken orally; some posters mention it in combination with other compounds. Specific dosing is a matter for a prescriber.

Common effects include sedation, dizziness and dry mouth, and rarer effects include confusion, tremor and liver or blood problems. It is prescription-only in the US and Canada and over the counter in the UK. Appetite-stimulation claims about height are not supported by the cited literature.

chain: Weight and, with training, muscle gain
angle.text: People who find it hard to eat enough use appetite stimulation to support a gaining phase, with the physique result depending on diet and training.

lead: Cyproheptadine (brand name Periactin) is a first-generation H1 antihistamine with strong serotonin 5-HT2 antagonist activity, patented in 1959 and introduced medically in 1961 [1]. Increased appetite and weight gain are known effects, and clinicians use it off-label to stimulate appetite in underweight children and people with conditions such as cystic fibrosis [1][2].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it is discussed as an appetite aid for people trying to gain weight or muscle, and sometimes in height-related talk [3][4]. A 2019 systematic review found that 39 of 46 included articles reported significant weight gain [2].

paras: Cyproheptadine blocks histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and has anticholinergic and antidopaminergic properties; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes sedation [1]. Medical off-label uses include serotonin syndrome, antipsychotic-induced akathisia and migraine prevention in some countries [1][5][6].

The 2019 Appetite systematic review covered 21 treatment populations and 32 randomized trials; most studies showed weight gain [2]. An early randomized trial in anorexia nervosa found weight gain in a particular subgroup of patients [7]. Pediatric trials in cancer cachexia and feeding disorders have been registered, several terminated early [8][9][10].
Reported effects include sedation, dizziness, confusion, tremor, hypotension, dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention; rare effects are liver problems, blood disorders and anaphylaxis [1].

On T Nation, members discuss appetite stimulants and cyproheptadine for people who struggle to eat; one thread notes it as an ingredient in some foreign-made anabolic products [3][4]. A looksmax.org thread discusses it within Ray Peat-inspired approaches combined with other compounds [11]. Claims about height or growth hormone in these discussions are community claims, and the cited literature describes appetite and weight effects.

A 2019 systematic review of 46 articles (32 randomized trials) reported significant weight gain in 39 [2]. A 1979 randomized trial in 81 anorexia nervosa patients found weight gain in a subgroup [7]. Registered trials include NCT00066248 in children with cancer-related weight loss [9].
